where: Section 2, third bullet ('Some syllabi call Ls the commutating reactance')
problem: Reactance is ωLs, measured in ohms; Ls is an inductance in henries. The worked example (step 2) correctly calls ωLs = 0.3142 Ω the commutating reactance, so this bullet contradicts the example and can make a student put henries into a formula that expects ohms.
fix: Some syllabi call ωLs the commutating reactance and quote the drop as a per-unit reactance, x = ωLs/Zbase, scaled by a base impedance Zbase.

problem: 'The bridge shorts the supply' is loose and misleading. In commutation failure the current fails to transfer, the outgoing device keeps conducting, two devices of the same leg conduct together, and it is the DC link that is shorted (giving a large overcurrent). The AC supply itself is not shorted.
fix: Push α higher and commutation failure follows: the current fails to transfer, both devices of a leg conduct together and the DC link is shorted, so a large overcurrent flows.

where: Section 1 definition of Ls and the single-phase drop formula in Section 2 (also used in Q3 and Q4)
problem: Ls is defined as the source inductance per line, but the single-phase formula 2ωLs Idc/π comes from taking Ls as the whole commutating inductance of the loop. In a single-phase bridge the source current path runs out through one line and back through the other, so a per-line Ls gives a loop inductance of 2Ls and a drop of 4ωLs Idc/π. As printed, a student who reads 'per line' literally will be out by a factor of 2 (with 2 mH per line and 10 A, the derivation gives about 23°, not the quoted 16°). The three-phase formula is consistent with per-phase Ls.
fix: State the convention: for the single-phase bridge 2ωLs Idc/π applies when Ls is the total commutating inductance of the loop; if Ls is per line, the loop has 2Ls and the drop is 4ωLs Idc/π. Alternatively, keep the per-line definition and write the single-phase drop as 4ωLs Idc/π.
